attributes.title: A Middle Way proposal towards an equitable open access publishing model
attributes.description: Open access promised to widen participation in science, but the article-processing charge (APC) that funds much of gold open access has shifted the cost of publishing onto authors, reproducing rather than removing exclusion for the Global South. Writing as a journal editor based in Brazil, I argue that the instruments now relied upon, namely fee waivers, purchasing-power-parity pricing and transformative agreements, are each useful but insufficient, because each treats a structural problem as a matter of discounting. Latin America's non-commercial diamond model, exemplified by SciELO, has shown that affordable open access is achievable at roughly a tenth of the cost of a commercial APC, yet it remains constrained by limited global visibility. I propose a “Middle Way”: a public–private model in which national governments fund and own the core publishing infrastructure as a public good, as Brazil is now doing through the nationalisation of SciELO, while commercial firms are contracted, on transparent and unbundled terms, for the services they perform better, chiefly discoverability and global distribution. Ownership stays public, and the commercial sector becomes a contracted supplier rather than the owner of the venue. The proposal's scope condition is ownership: it fits systems where the publishing venue is, or can become, publicly or institutionally owned.
attributes.conflict_of_interest_statement: I have held honorary and temporary editorial roles with Wiley, including senior editorships at Wiley journals, since before the 2024 talk on which this article is based, and since June 2026 I have been employed full-time as a Deputy Editor at Wiley. I conceived this article, and delivered the underlying talk, before that full-time appointment. The views expressed are my own and do not represent those of Wiley or any affiliated entity.

attributes.title: Open Here, There and Everywhere? A Comparative Review of Open Access Definitions and Typologies in Monitoring Instruments
attributes.description: Open Access (OA) monitoring has become a policy instrument for governments, institutions, and research funders globally, yet the typologies and definitions underlying OA monitors have never been systematically compared. Drawing on a global dataset of 30 OA monitors, we conduct the first systematic comparative review of their operational OA definitions and typologies. Our findings reveal dynamics of standardization, as well as enduring differences. Unpaywall/OpenAlex occupies a near-hegemonic position as metadata provider (77% of monitors), shaping classification choices across the landscape. Nevertheless, significant heterogeneity persists: monitors diverge on whether Bronze publications constitute true OA, on how to count Green OA publications, on the relevance of open licenses, and on whether economic dimensions (APCs, Diamond OA) belong in typologies at all. Only two monitors share both a common typology and identical operational criteria. These divergences pose challenges for cross-national comparability and call for greater methodological transparency in open science monitoring infrastructures.
